quickAnswer: Lincoln ranks 3rd of the 50 towns we serve for median home value ($1,184,800) and 3rd for homes built since 2010 (17.2%), yet 61.1% of its homes predate 1980 (ACS 2022). Old and new equipment sit side by side, and utility gas heats 55.1% of occupied homes.
body: ## Expensive homes, new construction and a large rental market

The Census Bureau's 2022 American Community Survey (ACS) puts the median owner-occupied home in Lincoln at $1,184,800, the 3rd-highest value among the 50 towns we serve, against $579,150 for the middle town. Newer building stands out as well: 467 of the town's 2,718 housing units (17.2%) went up since 2010, also 3rd of 50, and 772 (28.4%) are from 2000 or later. The middle town has 8.4% built since 2010.

The older stock is just as large. The median home dates from 1973, and 1,662 units (61.1%) predate 1980. Within that group, 731 (26.9%) are from 1960 to 1979, 534 (19.6%) from 1940 to 1959 and 397 (14.6%) from 1939 or earlier. Houses from the 2000s on were generally built under tighter energy rules than houses from the 1960s, so the two groups can call for different equipment. Value alone does not size a system; the heating load of the building does.
## Gas, oil and electric heat

Utility gas heats 1,411 occupied homes (55.1%), the 17th-highest share, against 41.9% for the middle town. Fuel oil or kerosene heats 602 (23.5%), ranking 39th, while electricity heats 397 (15.5%), ranking 12th. Bottled gas serves 113 homes (4.4%) and wood 17 (0.7%). In a gas home, a replacement is often a like-for-like comparison of models and efficiency levels. The 602 oil homes and 113 bottled-gas homes face a different question, because their fuel arrives by truck.
## The southeast corner of Concord

Wikipedia says Europeans settled Lincoln in 1654 as part of Concord, and that the town was formed by splitting off a substantial piece of southeast Concord and was incorporated in 1754. Because it was made of pieces taken from Concord, Weston and Lexington, it was sometimes called "Niptown." Chambers Russell, who was influential in creating the town, named it after his family home in Lincolnshire, England, and his homestead later became known as the Codman House property. Paul Revere was captured by British soldiers in Lincoln on the night of April 18, 1775.

The town covers 15.0 square miles, of which 14.4 are land and 0.6 are water (4.26%), and Wikipedia notes a sizeable amount of public conservation land. A house from the colonial era or the 19th century predates modern insulation, and old framing often leaks heat in ways a newer house does not. Lincoln has 397 units from 1939 or earlier (14.6%), 31st of 50 on that measure, a smaller share than the middle town's 16.6%.
## Renters, townhouses and small apartment buildings

Renters hold 914 households (35.7%), the 5th-highest share of the 50 towns, against 16.4% for the middle town. Detached houses are 1,589 units (58.5%), 39th of 50 and well under the 76.7% of the middle town. Another 577 units (21.2%) are attached townhouses, 162 (6.0%) sit in buildings of 3 or 4 units and 348 (12.8%) in buildings with 5 or more. Vacancy is 5.7%, 155 units, the 8th-highest rate.

For rentals, the State Sanitary Code sets a floor of 64 F overnight and 68 F between 7 a.m. and 11 p.m. during the heating season (105 CMR 410.201), and the landlord pays for heat unless the lease says otherwise. That is general information, not legal advice.
## Which rebates, and from whom

Heat pump rebates run through the electric utility that serves each address, so confirm which utility serves yours before planning around a rebate. The [heat pump page](/cities/lincoln/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits) lays out what we can say about Lincoln.

faq.q: Should I replace a gas furnace or boiler in Lincoln with a heat pump?
faq.a: A like-for-like gas replacement is the simpler project, and 1,411 Lincoln homes (55.1%) start from gas. A heat pump can still make sense, especially where cooling is wanted too. The right answer depends on how well the house holds heat, so we assess the heating load before quoting any system.

faq.q: Does the age of my Lincoln home matter for equipment size?
faq.a: Yes. Lincoln has 731 homes from 1960 to 1979 and 772 from 2000 or later, and their insulation and air leakage can differ a lot. Two houses with the same floor area may need very different capacity, which is why size should come from the building rather than the square footage.

faq.q: Do you work on townhouses and small apartment buildings?
faq.a: Yes, we serve homes and businesses. Lincoln has 577 attached townhouses and 552 units in multi-unit buildings, and shared walls or a shared boiler change the plan. The unit, the way heat is distributed and who owns the equipment all need sorting out before a quote makes sense.

faq.q: What should I do if the heat fails at night?
faq.a: Call (508) 786-8755 at any hour, because we take emergency calls around the clock. If you rent, tell the landlord promptly as well, since the landlord normally pays for heat. Do not bypass safety controls on a gas or oil burner to get heat back.

heating-installation-repair.quickAnswer: Utility gas heats 1,411 occupied homes in Lincoln, with 602 on oil and 397 on electricity, so a heating replacement starts from a different fuel at different addresses. Gas equipment also brings a permit and an inspection.
body: ## Starting from the fuel you have

The 2022 ACS counts 1,411 Lincoln homes on utility gas, 602 on oil or kerosene, 397 on electricity, 113 on bottled gas and 17 on wood, with 12 on other fuels or coal and 11 reporting no heating fuel. A gas home can swap a furnace or boiler for the same fuel type with the least change. An oil or bottled-gas home has more room to choose, since a gas connection, a heat pump or new oil equipment all stay on the table.
### Permits for gas equipment

Only licensed plumbers and gas fitters can pull gas permits in Massachusetts, and a new gas furnace or boiler normally needs a permit and a final inspection. Ask the building department how it handles applications. Venting and gas piping usually take as much planning as the appliance.
### Age of the house

Lincoln has 1,662 homes (61.1%) built before 1980, a little above the 57.2% of the middle town, and the median home dates from 1973. An old boiler or furnace can be oversized for a house that has since gained insulation and new windows, so a replacement should be sized from the house as it stands.
### Townhouses and multi-unit buildings

There are 577 attached townhouses and 162 units in buildings of 3 or 4 units in town. In shared buildings, the answer to what to replace depends on whether each unit has its own furnace or boiler or several units share one. A shared boiler is an owner or association decision, and a planned swap in late summer avoids a January emergency.
### Repair or replace

A fault in one part on a fairly young system is usually a repair. Frequent breakdowns, a leaking boiler section or a cracked heat exchanger point to replacement. Weigh the repair against the years left in the equipment, not just against the price of a new unit.
Also see the [maintenance page](/cities/lincoln/hvac-maintenance-tune-ups) for what a yearly visit covers.

faq.q: Is it worth converting an oil boiler to gas in Lincoln?
faq.a: It can be, where a gas main already serves the street. Gas is the main fuel in town, 55.1% of homes, but each address differs. Compare the connection cost, the new boiler and the permit against a new oil boiler or a heat pump before deciding.

faq.q: Furnace or boiler: which one should I choose?
faq.a: The existing distribution usually decides. A house with ducts suits a furnace, and a house with radiators or baseboards suits a boiler. Switching from one to the other means new ductwork or new piping, so it usually makes sense mainly during a major renovation.

faq.q: My house was built from 1960 to 1979; what changes?
faq.a: Lincoln has 731 homes from 1960 to 1979, and their original equipment may be well past its expected life. Insulation upgrades since then can leave an old unit oversized. Ask for the heating load to be assessed first, then compare sizes against the old nameplate.

air-conditioning-installation-repair.quickAnswer: Lincoln mixes 1,589 detached houses with 577 townhouses and 552 units in multi-unit buildings, so cooling plans vary. Central systems fit homes with good ductwork, and ductless mini-splits fit those without it.
body: ## Cooling a town with several kinds of housing

Detached houses make up 58.5% of Lincoln's housing in the 2022 ACS, ranking 39th of 50, while the middle town sits at 76.7%. Townhouses are 21.2%, and 552 units (20.3%) are in multi-unit buildings. Detached owners usually have the most freedom to place a central condenser. In a townhouse or condo building, outdoor space and association rules narrow the choices.
### Newer homes

Lincoln has 772 homes from 2000 or later (28.4%) and 467 since 2010 (17.2%). A house from those years is likelier than a house from 1940 to 1959 to have ductwork planned with cooling in mind, which may make a central system or a replacement compressor straightforward. Whether a given house has it is something to check on site, not assume.
### The thinnest age band

Only 284 Lincoln homes (10.4%) date from 1980 to 1999, the smallest age band. Cooling choices therefore split between the mid-century houses (731 from 1960 to 1979) and the 2000-and-later group, rather than clustering around one era.
### Older homes without ducts

The median Lincoln home was built in 1973, and 534 homes date from 1940 to 1959. Many homes of that vintage were built before central air was common. If heat comes from radiators or baseboards, a ductless mini-split can cool without opening walls: one outdoor unit and one or more small indoor heads.
### Electric heat

Electricity heats 397 Lincoln homes (15.5%), the 12th-highest share. A heat pump can serve those homes in both seasons, so a new cooling purchase doubles as a heating upgrade. The rebate path depends on the electric utility serving the address; see the [heat pump page](/cities/lincoln/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits).
### Sizing and common faults

Oversizing is the usual mistake: a unit that is too large cools fast, cycles off and leaves moisture in the air. A hot house after a few seasons can also mean low refrigerant, a dirty coil or a weak capacitor, and each has a different fix. A dead compressor in an old unit often tips the decision toward replacement.

faq.q: Can a Lincoln townhouse get air conditioning?
faq.a: Usually yes. Ductless cooling needs only a thin refrigerant line to the outdoor unit, which suits attached homes. Check the association's rules on outdoor equipment, and plan the unit's placement away from neighbors' windows to keep noise down.

faq.q: How many mini-split heads does a house need?
faq.a: It depends on layout and on how many rooms you want cooled. A single head can cover an open living area, while bedrooms behind closed doors may each need their own. Mass HVAC provides a free written estimate before work starts, so the head count is in writing.

faq.q: When is repairing a central air conditioner not worth it?
faq.a: When the compressor fails on an old unit, or when repairs keep recurring. A modest part, such as a capacitor, is a repair. Ask how much service life is left in the outdoor unit and coil, then compare that with a replacement sized to the house.

heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits.quickAnswer: The utility serving each Lincoln address decides the rebate path, so confirm it first. Lincoln has 772 homes built in 2000 or later and 397 electrically heated homes, and its fuel mix includes 602 oil homes.
body: ## Heat pumps in Lincoln

Where an address qualifies through its electric utility, the 2026 whole-home rebate is $2,650 per ton, up to $8,500 per home, and the house must be weatherized first. Our [general heat pump page](/services/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits) has the full conditions.
### The weatherization test against Lincoln's ages

The age route covers homes built in 2000 or later, which in Lincoln means 772 units (28.4%), including 467 built since 2010. The 1,662 homes (61.1%) built before 1980 more likely start with a Home Energy Assessment. Lincoln ranks 3rd of 50 for the share built since 2010,.
### Which fuel a heat pump replaces

Utility gas heats 1,411 homes, and a heat pump there is compared with a fuel that arrives by pipe, which is a different decision than for oil or bottled gas. The 602 oil homes and 113 bottled-gas homes depend on deliveries, and a heat pump can displace part or all of that. In the 397 electrically heated homes, a heat pump would replace resistance heat, moving heat instead of generating it.
### Townhouses, condos and ductless

With 577 attached townhouses and 552 units in multi-unit buildings, townhouses and condo units often have limited outdoor space. Ductless heads on an interior wall and a compact outdoor unit can fit where a ducted system would not. In a detached house with sound ducts, a ducted heat pump may reuse them.
### Two housing stocks, two loads

Lincoln's 1,662 homes built before 1980 and its 772 built since 2000 do not need the same capacity. A heat pump sized for a leaky house from 1960 to 1979 would be oversized for a tight house from the 2010s, which is why sizing house by house matters more than the brand.
### Keeping a backup
A hybrid setup keeps the existing gas or oil system for the coldest days and lets the heat pump carry milder weather. It can ease the move for owners who want a second source.
Our [heating page](/cities/lincoln/heating-installation-repair) sets a heat pump beside a straight boiler or furnace swap.

faq.q: How do I find out which utility serves my Lincoln address?
faq.a: Your electric bill names it. The rebate path depends on that utility, and the amounts and conditions on masssave.com can change. Confirm the utility and the terms before you plan a budget around a rebate.

faq.q: Does a newer Lincoln house skip the assessment?
faq.a: A home built in 2000 or later passes the weatherization test by age, which describes 772 units here. Older homes need a Home Energy Assessment recommending little work, or completed recommendations. Air leakage also affects the size of heat pump a house needs.

faq.q: Can a heat pump replace gas heat in Lincoln?
faq.a: Often it can carry most of the load, but the answer depends on the house. Gas heats 55.1% of Lincoln homes, so many owners will compare a pipe-delivered fuel against a heat pump. Sizing, insulation and the coldest nights all matter, and a hybrid is an option.

hvac-maintenance-tune-ups.quickAnswer: Gas heats 1,411 Lincoln homes and oil 602, so most tune-ups here are gas safety checks, with a smaller group needing a yearly oil cleaning. Rentals, empty homes and heat pumps each have their own routine.
body: ## What a yearly service looks like in Lincoln

- **Utility gas, 1,411 homes:** the burner, venting and controls are inspected for safe, efficient operation.
- **Oil, 602 homes:** soot is cleaned from the burner and boiler or furnace, the nozzle and filter are swapped and combustion is measured.
- **Bottled gas, 113 homes:** gas checks plus a look at the regulator and piping.
- **Electric and heat pump homes, 397:** filters, coils, drain and refrigerant side.
- **Wood, 17 homes:** a stove does not remove the need to look after any boiler or furnace beside it.
### Renters and landlords

Lincoln has 914 renter households, the 5th-highest share among the 50 towns. A boiler or furnace that fails in a cold snap affects tenants first, and a tune-up in early fall is a practical way to lower that risk.
### Empty and part-time homes

The ACS counts 155 vacant units in Lincoln (5.7%), the 8th-highest vacancy rate, against 3.6% for the middle town. A home that sits empty for weeks can still need a start-up check, a look at condensate drains and a filter change before the heating season. Water left standing in a drain pan is a common cause of odors.
### New equipment and old equipment

With 467 homes built since 2010, some Lincoln systems are young. A young system still needs filters, coils and drains looked after. At the other end, systems in houses built from 1960 to 1979 benefit from a combustion and safety check before each winter.
### Attached homes and shared equipment

Lincoln has 577 attached townhouses. Where several homes share a boiler or a row of outdoor condensers sits along a wall, servicing is simpler when the owner or association books it for the whole group on one schedule.
### Seasonal rhythm

- **Early fall:** heating checks.
- **Late spring:** cooling and mini-split service.
- **Any time:** a new smell, repeated short cycling, soot or water around the equipment calls for an early visit.
The [indoor air page](/cities/lincoln/indoor-air-quality) covers filters and humidity, and the [heating page](/cities/lincoln/heating-installation-repair) explains when a repair stops making sense.

faq.q: How often should a gas furnace or boiler be serviced?
faq.a: Once a year is the usual advice, before the heating season. The visit covers the burner, venting, controls and combustion. In a town where gas is the main fuel, that check is the one that touches the most homes.

faq.q: Do oil systems need a different schedule?
faq.a: They need the same yearly timing but a longer job. Oil leaves soot, so the burner and heat exchanger are cleaned and the nozzle and filter are replaced. Lincoln has 602 oil homes, a smaller but real group whose boilers rely on that annual cleaning.

faq.q: Does a vacant or seasonal property need a tune-up?
faq.a: Often yes. Equipment that has not run for months can have dry drains, stale filters and settled dust. Lincoln has 155 vacant units, and a start-up check before the first cold week is easier than finding a problem on the coldest night.

indoor-air-quality.quickAnswer: Lincoln's housing runs from 397 units built in 1939 or earlier to 772 built in 2000 or later. Leaky old houses and tight new ones need different ventilation, filtration and moisture control.
body: ## Air in old houses and new ones

The 2022 ACS sorts Lincoln's homes into 397 units from 1939 or earlier, 534 from 1940 to 1959, 731 from 1960 to 1979, 284 from 1980 to 1999 and 772 from 2000 or later. A house from before 1960 and a house from the 2010s breathe differently, so the same filter and fan plan will not suit both.
### Older houses

Old framing leaks, which exchanges air but also lets in dust, pollen and damp from the crawlspace or basement. Materials from older decades can matter during renovation, and a qualified specialist should test before work disturbs them. Lincoln has 1,662 units from before 1980.
### Tight new houses

A house built since 2010 (467 in Lincoln) is generally tight, so cooking fumes, moisture and chemicals from furnishings do not leak out on their own. A range hood that vents outdoors, working bath fans and sometimes a dedicated ventilator manage that. Humidity can climb in summer without a dehumidifying cooling system.
### Shared walls

Shared buildings are a feature of the housing here, 552 units in all. Odors, smoke and cooking fumes can travel between neighboring units in shared buildings, and air sealing between units can help. An owner or association usually decides on changes to shared ductwork.
### Empty homes and moisture

With 155 vacant units, damp can build in homes that nobody heats or ventilates. A hygrometer shows whether the air is too humid before you buy a dehumidifier. If readings stay high, find the source of the water first.
### Water on the map

Wikipedia gives Lincoln 0.6 square miles of water (4.26% of its area). A damp cellar still depends on the individual house and how water drains around it, so test the air with a hygrometer instead of assuming.
### Options

- Upgrade filtration and change filters on schedule.
- Match a humidifier or dehumidifier to the system.
- Add or repair mechanical ventilation in tight homes.
- Clean ducts only when they are visibly dirty or damaged.
The [maintenance page](/cities/lincoln/hvac-maintenance-tune-ups) covers routine filter and coil care.

faq.q: Should I test for radon or mold?
faq.a: Mold shows up as a smell or a visible stain, and a moisture meter helps find its source. Radon is a different question, answered with a test kit or a professional. Neither is solved by a filter, so deal with the cause rather than the air.

faq.q: Is a tight house always better?
faq.a: A tight house wastes less heat but traps pollutants unless it has ventilation. Lincoln has 467 homes built since 2010, the 3rd-highest share among the 50 towns. Those homes often benefit from fresh-air ventilation and from kitchen and bath fans that vent outdoors.

faq.q: Do I need my ducts cleaned?
faq.a: Not automatically. Dust blowing from registers, visible mold or a renovation are good reasons. Without one, filters and sealed ducts usually do more than a cleaning. Ask for a camera or visual inspection first, then decide whether cleaning would change anything.
